10. Comparability Over Time and Space

Data from individual weather stations were averaged to determine national and state-level annual values for the length of growing season. To provide spatial representativeness, national and state-level values were computed using a spatially weighted average, and, as a result, stations in low-station-density areas make a larger contribution to the national or state average than stations in high-density areas.

GCMs inherently use consistent algorithms over time and space.

Observed and projected series reflect the same indicator definition, although the former are naturally derived from station data, while the latter are derived from a grid.

11. Data Limitations

The technical documentation for the Length of Growing Season indicator identifies some factors that may impact the confidence, application, or conclusions that readers can draw from the observed portion of this pairing. The documentation acknowledges that changes in measurement techniques and instruments over time can affect trends but notes that these data were carefully reviewed for quality, and values that appeared to be invalid or outliers were not included in the final compilation. This data set includes only data from weather stations that did not have many missing data points.

Future projections of any variable have inherent uncertainty, as described in Section 12 below.

12. Sources of Uncertainty

Observations inevitably reflect measurement uncertainty. Kunkel et al. (2004) present uncertainty measurements for an earlier (but mostly similar) version of the national analyses. To test worst-case conditions, Kunkel et al. (2004) computed growing season trends for a thinned-out subset of stations across the country, attempting to simulate the density of the portions of the country with the lowest overall station density. The 95 percent confidence intervals for the resulting trend in length of growing season were ±2 days. Thus, there is a very high likelihood that observed changes in growing season are real and not artifacts of sampling error.

Model outputs inevitably reflect model uncertainty. Each GCM represents aspects of, and processes within, the climate system differently. These differences will lead to differences in how the GCMs represent both present-day climate and how the climate responds to changes in greenhouse gases. For example, GCMs differ in climate sensitivity, defined as the increase in global temperature when carbon dioxide in the atmosphere doubles relative to pre-industrial times. Even a single GCM will yield different results if presented with different initial conditions, as the chaotic processes within the model will lead to different timing of various modes of variability within the model (such as the El Niño cycle). The shaded bands in the graph for this pairing illustrate this type of uncertainty in the spread of models, as well as year-to-year variations due to internal variability within each model.

Interpreting projections also requires users to consider scenario uncertainty. Projecting future conditions requires assumptions about future greenhouse gas emissions. This feature presents four widely used scenarios to illustrate a range of possibilities without assigning likelihoods to them, nor do these scenarios necessarily bound possible futures.

The choice of downscaling approach introduces a source of uncertainty relating to the technique and data used in the downscaling model. However, this uncertainty is typically smaller than the uncertainty stemming from the spread in climate models and scenario uncertainty (e.g., Lafferty and Sriver, 2023; Wooten et al., 2017).

13. Sources of Variability

At any given location, the timing of spring and fall frosts naturally varies from year to year as a result of normal variation in weather patterns, multi-year climate cycles such as the El Niño–Southern Oscillation and Pacific Decadal Oscillation, and other factors. The construction of this pairing addresses variability in a few ways:

  • Presenting a long-term data set and calculating spatial averages.
  • Smoothing GCM outputs with an 11-year moving average.
